title: Is AI Feedback True but Useless?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: This article reports on a large-scale study involving nearly 9,000 Year 6 students across 211 schools who received a mix of human and AI feedback on creative writing redrafts, examining whether AI-generated feedback actually improves student writing. Daisy Christodoulou frames the study around a classic problem in feedback research: the risk of 'TBU' feedback — true but useless — illustrated by Dylan Wiliam's anecdote of a student who received the comment 'make your scientific investigations more systematic' and simply replied that if he knew how to be more systematic, he would already have been. The study found an average effect size of 0.2 (about 8 scaled score points), a meaningful improvement — but 36% of students actually got worse scores on the redraft, raising important questions about what distinguishes improvers from decliners. The piece introduces a novel feedback format — personalised multiple-choice questions rather than written comments — as Christodoulou's hypothesis for making feedback more actionable rather than merely accurate.
points: AI-generated feedback is now easy to produce at scale — personalized written comments for thousands of students — but the central research question remains whether students actually read it, understand it, act on it, and permanently change their mental models as a result.

The 'true but useless' (TBU) problem applies to AI feedback exactly as it applies to human feedback: a comment can be accurate and specific yet still fail to tell a student how to implement the change, leaving them no better equipped than before.

A 0.2 effect size improvement across 9,000 students is statistically meaningful, but the finding that 36% of students actually declined on the redraft is equally important — it demands investigation of what differentiates improvers from decliners.

Personalised multiple-choice questions may prove more actionable than written feedback because they constrain the response space and force engagement with specific dimensions of craft rather than leaving students to decode abstract comments.

The fact that improving sentence structure had a material impact on writing quality and reader understanding in the most-improved students suggests that the type and specificity of feedback (targeted at concrete skill dimensions) matters more than its volume.
quotes: Last term we completed a large-scale writing redraft project. Nearly 9,000 Year 6 students (10-11 year olds) from 211 schools took part in a two-stage writing assessment. First, they wrote a creative response to an image prompt in independent conditions. Second, a couple of weeks later they received a mix of human and AI feedback on their writing, and redrafted their response.

It is now relatively easy to use AI to produce reams of polished and personalised written feedback for a student. In some ways this is incredible: as I have written before, if I had had this technology when I started teaching, it would have been transformative.

But there is still a big research question about the effectiveness of written feedback. Do students read it? If they read it, do they understand it? If they understand it, do they act on it? And if they act on it, does it permanently change their mental models?

Dylan Wiliam has a great anecdote where he sees that a student has received the feedback 'you need to make your scientific investigations more systematic.' He asks the student what he is going to do differently as a result. The student replies 'I don't know. If I knew how to be more systematic, I would have been so the first time.' This is the problem with all written feedback, whoever writes it. It risks being TBU — true but useless.

We have the headline results from the assessment, and they show that the cohort improved by 8 scaled score points — an effect size of about 0.2. This is a significant and meaningful improvement. However, not all students improved! Only 64% got a better score on the second assessment. The rest went backwards.

Our hunch is these will be more useful than the comments, but we need to do more work to test this. As well as the traditional written comment, we also provide schools with an examiner's report for the teacher, and with a set of personalised multiple-choice questions for each student.
